gallery.title: Size & growth
gallery.blurb:
How much research is there, and what kind? 44,941 health economic evaluations were
             extracted (2010–2026); 38,199 are eligible for analysis. These panels carry the headline:
             the growth of the corpus, and how its evaluation-method mix has shifted.

figs.title: Cumulative growth
figs.caption:
The field keeps doubling: half of everything published since 2010 appeared
                      after 2020 (2026 flagged partial).

figs.title: Evaluation-method composition over time
figs.caption:
Cost-utility rose from 45% to 54% of annual output while cost-effectiveness
                      fell from 34% to 25%.

gallery.title: Topics & diseases
gallery.blurb:
Topic, disease and intervention — the subject of the evidence. OpenAlex topics cover
             88% of the corpus; MeSH disease groups cover 63% (harvested subset, base declared on
             each figure). The emergent-theme maps come from abstract embeddings, not MeSH.

figs.title: Topic landscape
figs.caption:
OpenAlex subfields grouped by field — the research areas of the field in
                      one circular view.

figs.title: Disease landscape
figs.caption: MeSH disease groups: share of studies, coloured by LMIC/HIC lean.

figs.title: Disease × evaluation method
figs.caption:
How each disease area is evaluated — cost-utility vs cost-effectiveness
                      heat map.

figs.title: Epidemiological transition of research
figs.caption:
LMIC research shifted communicable → NCD past the burden shares; injuries
                      stayed at ~1% of research vs 11% of burden.

figs.title: Thematic landscape by income
figs.caption:
Embedding topic map (UMAP + HDBSCAN) coloured by each theme's LMIC share:
                      theme space segregates — malaria 91% LMIC vs dementia 6%.

figs.title: Thematic landscape
figs.caption: The plain theme-space map of the corpus, before income colouring.

figs.title: Emergent themes ranked by income
figs.caption:
The 15 most- and 15 least-LMIC themes: the two ends never overlap
                      (33–91% vs 3–13% LMIC).

gallery.title: Methods & decision-usefulness
gallery.blurb:
What gets measured, and how well — the decision-usefulness core. How evidence flows
             from design to method to outcome, which comparable metric is used where, and whether
             abstracts foreground the elements a decision-maker needs.

figs.title: Source → analysis → outcome
figs.caption:
Alluvial of design basis → evaluation type → outcome family: how evidence
                      flows through the field.

figs.title: The comparable-metric currency
figs.caption:
QALYs for rich settings, DALYs for poor: cross-income comparability is
                      broken at the metric level.

figs.title: Model vs measurement over 17 years
figs.caption:
The drift toward model-based (vs directly measured) evaluations, by income
                      group.

figs.title: Decision-framing in abstracts
figs.caption:
ICER 39%, threshold 22%: few abstracts foreground decision elements — and
                      LMIC studies report them slightly more than HIC, not less.

figs.title: What predicts decision-usefulness
figs.caption:
Adjusted odds ratios: income, design basis, disease and year predict
                      generic-metric use. Observational, never causal.

gallery.title: Geography & authorship
gallery.blurb:
Where the research is about, and who leads it. Income-comparative figures use
             extracted geography only (the affiliation proxy is income-biased in availability).

figs.title: Global proportional-symbol map
figs.caption:
Where the evidence sits: bubbles by country study count, coloured by income
                      group (Berrang-Ford style, Robinson).

figs.title: World map of output
figs.caption: The global distribution of eligible evaluations by country.

figs.title: Top producers: volume vs per-capita
figs.caption: Two-rank slope — who leads by count vs by output per person.

figs.title: Who leads research about each setting
figs.caption:
Local / mixed / foreign authorship stacked by income: research about poor
                      countries is often led from abroad.

figs.title: Collaboration structure
figs.caption:
Income × income co-authorship chord: how the collaboration network runs
                      between groups.

gallery.title: Gaps vs disease burden
gallery.blurb:
The map's whole point: research vs the burden of disease (GBD 2023 DALYs, country
             totals and 22 Level-2 causes) and vs health spending (IHME, PPP 2022).

figs.title: Evidence per unit of burden
figs.caption:
Studies per 100k DALYs vs total burden: an 18× gap between the best- and
                      worst-served countries.

figs.title: Evidence per dollar of spending
figs.caption:
Studies per US$1bn of health spending (PPP 2022 × latest World Bank
                      population, mostly 2025).

figs.title: Research share vs burden share, by disease
figs.caption:
Maternal-neonatal research runs at 3.6× its burden share in HIC vs 0.37× in
                      LMIC; injuries 0.21× in LMIC.

figs.title: Burden-weighted disease mismatch (journal finish)
figs.caption: The same mismatch in Lancet register: study share vs DALY share by income.

figs.title: Largest absolute evidence deficits
figs.caption:
Studies vs burden-expected: India +4,847 short, Nigeria +1,205,
                      Indonesia +920 …

figs.title: High burden, low research
figs.caption:
The burden × evidence plane with a burden-proportional diagonal; size =
                      population. The editorial closer.

figs.title: Within-LMIC inequality
figs.caption:
Lorenz curve: the least-served half of LMIC burden holds 16% of the
                      evidence; top 5 countries hold 55%; Gini 0.50.

gallery.title: Open access & funding
gallery.blurb:
How the evidence is packaged and reached. Open-access status covers 93% of the
             eligible corpus (post DOI-supplement harvest); the funder field covers ~28% and is a
             floor, not a census.

figs.title: Open access over time
figs.caption: 46% → 80% (2010–24); LMIC research is more open than HIC research.

figs.title: Who funds it
figs.caption:
Top funders by studies, split by income focus: most big funders are
                      HIC-focused; Gates dominates LMIC; Wellcome has a real LMIC share.

gallery.title: Country maps
gallery.blurb:
The cartographic collection: eligible-only counts, World Bank population, GBD 2023
             burden, extracted geography, Robinson projection. Share maps show only countries
             with ≥5 studies (grey below).

figs.title: Research intensity vs burden
figs.caption:
Studies per 100k DALYs, diverging scale — the map form of the burden
                      mismatch figure.

figs.title: Burden × evidence bivariate
figs.caption:
The high-burden/low-evidence corner lights up; dark purple is high on both
                      (big countries), not missing data.

figs.title: Evidence deserts
figs.caption:
0 / 1–5 / 6–20 / 21+ studies: 20 countries carry a burden but have no
                      evaluation at all.

figs.title: Who studies whom
figs.caption: Share of studies with a local author — parachute research, mapped.

figs.title: Model-based vs measured
figs.caption: The LMIC lean on modelled evidence, by country.

figs.title: Open access by country
figs.caption: Share of output that is open access (93% base).

figs.title: Where the evidence is youngest
figs.caption: Share of studies published since 2018.

figs.title: Dominant evaluation method
figs.caption: Cost-utility North / cost-effectiveness South.

figs.title: Disease atlas
figs.caption:
Eleven small-multiple maps, one per GBD disease group; log counts, so the
                      disease contrast is the point.

gallery.title: Trends over time
gallery.blurb:
Comparative time-series on the year dimension (2010–2025; 2026 partial, dropped).
             Income-comparative panels use single-country extracted geography with a known
             income group.

figs.title: Equity over time
figs.caption:
LMIC share of annual output rose 16% → 36% — still far below their 83%
                      burden share.

figs.title: QALY-metric convergence
figs.caption:
LMIC QALY use 15% → 49% vs HIC 51% → 59%: the gap narrowed, ~10pp
                      remains.

figs.title: Reach over time
figs.caption:
Cumulative share of each income group's countries with ≥1 evaluation:
                      high-income covered early, low-income reached last (28% → 96%).

figs.title: Method streamgraph
figs.caption:
Evaluation-type composition: cost-utility 45% → 54%, cost-effectiveness
                      34% → 25%.

figs.title: Decision-usefulness over time
figs.caption:
All four abstract signals rose; threshold most (12% → 29%) — still a
                      minority.

gallery.title: Priority-setting for funders
gallery.blurb:
Built for a funder asking where the next pound buys the most missing evidence.
             Ranked by gap, never by cost-to-close: there is no cost or research-funding-amount
             data. Proportionality to burden is a reference point, not a target.

figs.title: Opportunity matrix
figs.caption:
Disease × income research-to-burden ratio: injuries, maternal,
                      cardiovascular and neurological in lower-income settings are the reddest.

figs.title: Priority scorecard
figs.caption: Burden × intensity scatter plus the ranked deficit bar — the shortlist.

figs.title: Capacity-building quadrant
figs.caption:
Burden × local-authorship share: the high-burden, <75%-local set — fund
                      people, not just studies.

figs.title: Self-correcting vs stuck
figs.caption:
LMIC research-to-burden ratio, era-1 → era-2 arrows: injuries and maternal
                      are stuck below burden and worsening.

figs.title: Funder landscape
figs.caption:
Top funders by studies, split by income (~28% coverage — a floor, not a
                      census).

gallery.title: Journal figures
gallery.blurb:
The tight journal set: each figure carries one finding, greyscale-safe, legends
             present, uncertainty shown.

figs.title: PRISMA flow
figs.caption: Study selection: 44,941 extracted → 38,199 eligible evaluations.

figs.title: Decision-relevance cascade
figs.caption: Studies meeting each successive criterion for decision-relevance.

figs.title: Density within & between income groups
figs.caption:
Studies per 10 million people by country, faceted by income; area =
                      population.

figs.title: Disease composition by era and income
figs.caption: The epidemiological transition of the research, journal finish.

figs.title: Disease × income heat map
figs.caption: Which diseases dominate the evidence in each income group.

figs.title: In-country authorship
figs.caption:
Is the evidence produced in the countries it is about? Point + CI by
                      income.

figs.title: Evidence vs disease burden
figs.caption: Studies per 100k DALYs vs burden, by income — the 18× gap.

figs.title: Research attention vs burden, by disease
figs.caption: Study share vs DALY share across the 11 disease groups.

hero.text:
This app maps the global evidence base of health economic evaluations — studies that
             compare two or more ways of delivering care on both costs and consequences.
full economic evaluations are eligible for analysis. The

explains how the map is built.
